library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(readxl)
# Load data
df = read.csv("GrowthDJ.csv")
head(df)
nrow(df)
ncol(df)

df_clean <- na.omit(df)
head(df_clean)

ncol(df_clean)

class(df_clean$oil)

Cross Validation (CV)

Write a brief introduction to cross validation which includes relevant mathematical notation.
Answer: Cross validation is a statistical method used in machine learning to evaluate how well a model performs in an unseen or independent data set. It involves dividing the data set into multiple folds or subsets, using one of these folds as a validation set and training the model on the remaining folds. This process is then repeated multiple times each time using different fold as the validation set. The main purpose of cross validation is to prevent over fitting which occurs when a model is trained too well on the training data and performs poorly on new, unseen data
\(\mathrm{CV}(k) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^k \mathrm{MAE}_j\)



What is the goal of cross-validation? (Hint: Think about over-fitting, along with social/ethical considerations)
Answer: The goal of cross validation is to ensure that a model generalizes well beyond the data on which it was trained by repeatedly holding out different subsets fir testing, it guards against over fitting and produces an approximately unbiased estimate of out of sample error. This process not only helps in selecting and tuning models that truly capture underlying patterns rather than noise, but also promotes robustness and fairness: by validating across different folds.
What linear models are you considering based on your research question? Pick at least two models to compare.
Answer: I am considering two models. One model which is unadjusted model (model_1) which doesn’t contain confounders and another model which is adjusted model (model_2) that includes the confounders.

# Step 1: Model specification
lm_spec <- linear_reg() %>%
# Output Y is quantitative
set_mode("regression") %>%
# Want regression to be linear
set_engine("lm")



# Unadjusted model
model_1 <- lm_spec %>% fit(gdpgrowth ~ oil, data = df_clean)


# Adjusted model
model_2 <- lm_spec %>% fit(gdpgrowth ~ oil + school + invest, data = df_clean)


Explain how you divided your data into its test set and training set.
Answer: I split the data into two parts –a training set (80% of the observations) and a test set (the remaining 20%) so that we could both tune our models and then evaluate their performance on truly unseen data.

set.seed(2025)
split      <- initial_split(df_clean, prop = 0.8, strata = "oil")
train_data <- training(split)
test_data  <- testing(split)

State which error metric you are using (MAE or MSE) and give its formal mathematical definition. Why did you choose this error metric? What are the advantages/disadvantages of using it?
Answer: I will be using MAE. The formal mathematical definition is:
\(\mathrm{MAE} = \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n |y_i - \hat y_i|\)
I chose this error metric because it produces an error metric in the same units as the outcome which makes it immediately interpretable and it is also less sensitive to large outliers than the other error metric like MSE. The main advantage of MAE is the robustness to outliers. Since errors aren’t squared a few extreme misses don’t dominate the metric. Another advantage is that it’s easy to compute and understand which doesn’t require additional transformations.
However, it does have some drawbacks like MAE treats every error the same so one huge miss and several small misses can look equally bad even though we might just care about the big one.
Implement k-fold cross validation for k = 10.
Answer:

# 10-fold cross validation for model_1
set.seed(244)
model_1_cv <- lm_spec %>%
  fit_resamples(gdpgrowth~oil,
                resamples = vfold_cv(train_data, v = 10),
                metrics = metric_set(mae, rsq)
    )



# 10-fold cross validation for model_2
set.seed(253)
model_2_cv <- lm_spec %>%
  fit_resamples(
    gdpgrowth~oil+school+invest,
    resamples = vfold_cv(train_data, v = 10),
    metrics = metric_set(mae, rsq)
    )

# In sample MAE for model_2

Answer: 5-fold CV gave the lowest mean MAE, so we will use k=5.

Select your final model based on which one has the smallest CV error.
Answer: Model 2 has the smallest SV error compared to model 1. So, model_2 is my final model.



LASSO

Write a brief introduction to LASSO which includes relevant mathematical notation.
Answer: LASSO is a penalized regression method that shrinks coefficient estimates and performs variable selection.
\(\mathrm{RSS} + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j|\)

where lambda >= 0 is a tuning parameter controlling the strength of the L1 penalty. As lambda grows more coefficients are shrinking towards 0 or exactly to 0 which yields a model that is easier to interpret and often stable in the presence of multicollinearity. LASSO’s key advantages are it’s built in variable selection and improved predictive performance via regularization and it’s main drawback is potential bias in the non-zero coefficients due to shrinkage.

State which error metric you are using (i.e., CV MAE or CV MSE and state the chosen k-value).
Answer: I will be using CV MAE and k=10.
Identify at least p = 3 predictors X1, X2, …, Xp for modeling the expected response E(Y) of one of your variables Y.
Answer: For the LASSO model, I will predcit
\(Y= gdpgrowth\)
Using at least p=3 predictors.
\(X1 = gdp60\)
\(X2 = invest\)
\(X3 = school\)
Compute 50 LASSO models for 50 different values of 𝜆 (the penalty tuning parameter), each with all p predictors. You can start out by trying 𝜆 in the range of -5 to 1 on the log10 scale. Plot the cross-validated (CV) error for each value of 𝜆.
Answer:

# STEP 1: LASSO Algorithm & Model Specification
# This is copied exactly from the R Code Notes for LASSO Section
lasso_spec <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_mode("regression") %>%
  set_engine("glmnet") %>%
  set_args(mixture = 1, penalty = tune())



# STEP 2: Variable Recipe
variable_recipe <- recipe(gdpgrowth ~gdp60 + invest+ school , data = train_data) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())


# STEP 3: Workflow Specification (Model + Recipe)
# This is copied exactly from the R Code Notes for LASSO Section
lasso_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(variable_recipe) %>%
  add_model(lasso_spec)


# STEP 4: Estimate 50 LASSO models using
# lambda values on a "grid" or range from 10^(-5) to 10^(-0.1).
# Calculate the 10-fold CV MAE for each of the 50 models.
set.seed(123)
lasso_models<-lasso_workflow%>%
  tune_grid(
    grid= grid_regular(penalty(range=c(-5,1)),levels= 50 ),
    resamples= vfold_cv(train_data, v= 10 ),
    metrics= metric_set(mae)
    )


autoplot(lasso_models)+
  scale_x_continuous() +
  xlab(expression(lambda))


Based on your plot in the previous step, what value of lambda is best?
Answer: Based on my plot, when lambda = 0.34

# Checking the approximation with the code
best_penalty <- lasso_models %>%
  select_best(metric = "mae")
best_penalty

Pick the lambda associated with the parsimonious model.
Answer: 10

# This is copied exactly from the R Code Notes for LASSO Section
autoplot(lasso_models) +
  scale_x_continuous() +
  xlab(expression(lambda)) +
  geom_errorbar(data = collect_metrics(lasso_models),
                aes(x = penalty, ymin = mean- std_err, ymax = mean +
                      std_err), alpha = 0.5
                )



parsimonious_penalty <- lasso_models %>%
  select_by_one_std_err(metric = "mae", desc(penalty))
parsimonious_penalty


For your parsimonious model, how many and which predictors were kept?
Answer: For my parsimonious model, 4 variables were kept but rest of the other variables were shrunk exactly to zero. The variables that were kept are: gdp60, popgrowth, invest and inter_yes


final_lasso <- lasso_workflow %>%
  finalize_workflow(parameters = parsimonious_penalty) %>%
  fit(data = train_data)
final_lasso %>%

title: Lab: K-Means
text:
Getting Started






Download the .qmd file from Moodle and any needed .xlsx or .csv data files. Save these in the same folder/directory.
Open the Quarto file in RStudio: File > Open File... >. If you’re working on the MHC RStudio server, you need to upload the files first: go to the Files panel, then click Upload. Upload the .qmd file and any data files. You will need to upload each file one at a time.
Update the author and date in the YAML header of this file.
Click the Render button. If successful, you should have a new window pop up with a nice looking HTML document.
For this lab, you may need to still the package glmnet.

Ask for help if you encounter issues on any of the steps above. Once you’ve successfully made it through these steps, you can continue.




Load Packages
You likely will need to install some these packages before you can run the code chunk below successfully.

library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(factoextra)
library(amap)



Load Penguin Data

data(penguins)



Data Cleaning

# Remove missing values
# YOUR CODE HERE
penguins <- penguins %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(bill_length_mm) &
    !is.na(bill_depth_mm) &
    !is.na(species))

# Make data table (named penguins_reduced) that only has
# bill_length_mm and bill_depth_mm columns
penguins_reduced <- penguins  %>% select(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm)



Initial Visualization

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) + 
  geom_point() 








We’ll cluster these penguins based on their bill lengths and depths:


Implement \(K\)-Means
Complete the code below to run the K-means algorithm using K = 3.

set.seed(244)
# Run the K-means algorithm
kmeans_3_round_1 <- kmeans(scale(penguins_reduced), centers = 3) 
    
# Plot the cluster assignments
penguins_reduced %>% 
  mutate(kmeans_cluster = as.factor(kmeans_3_round_1$cluster)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = kmeans_cluster)) + 
  geom_point(size = 3) + 
  theme(legend.position = "none") + 
  labs(title = "K-means with K = 3 (round 1)") + 
  theme_minimal()









Why do we have to set the seed for K-means? In practice, why should we try out a variety of seeds?

Answer. For reproducibility. Every time we run the function kmeans, it initializes the centers of the clusters to be in random location. It’s possible that some random locations give better clustering results than others; since k-means is a greedy algorithm, it’s possible for it to have different results each time, and it’s possible for it to get “stuck” at a local solution.


K-Means Clusters Versus Known Species Groupings

  ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = species)) + 
  geom_point(size = 3) + 
  theme(legend.position = "none") + 
  labs(title = "Actual Groupings of Data Based on Species") + 
  theme_minimal()









Visually, how well do you think \(K\)-means captured the underlying species structure of the data?

Answer. I think it did pretty good! It found roughly the data points corresponding to each of the species groups, so it is identifying that as a way to structure the data.


Tuning \(K\)

To implement K-means clustering we must choose an appropriate K! Use the following example to see the two different extreme situations. Typically, the ideal \(K\) is somewhere between the two extremes.
Minimum: \(K = 2\) groups/clusters
Maximum: \(K = n\) groups/clusters (one observation per cluster)

What happens in the \(K\)-means algorithm if \(K = n\)?
Answer.
Let’s consider anywhere from \(K = 2\) to \(K = 20\) clusters.

set.seed(244)

k_2  <- kmeans(scale(penguins_reduced), centers = 2)
k_20 <- kmeans(scale(penguins_reduced), centers = 20)

penguins_reduced %>% 
  mutate(cluster_2 = as.factor(k_2$cluster)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = cluster_2)) + 
    geom_point(size = 3) + 
    labs(title = "K = 2")







penguins_reduced %>% 
  mutate(cluster_20 = as.factor(k_20$cluster)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = cluster_20)) + 
    geom_point(size = 3) + 
    labs(title = "K = 20") + 
    scale_color_manual(values = rainbow(20))








What are your general impressions?
Answer. YOUR ANSWER HERE


Finding Ideal K Value: Silhoutte

The average silhouette approach measures the quality of a clustering. That is, it determines how well each object lies within its cluster.

To do so, it maximizes the distance between clusters and minimizes distance within clusters.

A high average silhouette indicates a good clustering.
Given a range of possible K values, the optimal number of clusters (K) is the one that maximizes the average silhouette.

We can use a built-in silhouette method in the fviz_nbclust function to compute the average silhouette for various K values.

fviz_nbclust(scale(penguins_reduced), kmeans, method='silhouette')








Based on the average silhouette approach, what is the optimal \(K\) value?
Answer. The optimal value for \(K\) appears to be \(K\) = 3.


Experimenting with Distance Metrics
We can use the Kmeans method (notice the “K” is capitalized in this function name) from the amap library to specify how we are measuring distance in the K-means algorithm.

set.seed(244)
k_2_manattan = Kmeans(scale(penguins_reduced), centers = 3, 
                      method = "manhattan")
k_2_euclid = Kmeans(scale(penguins_reduced), centers = 3, 
                    method = "euclidean")
k_2_maxnorm = Kmeans(scale(penguins_reduced), centers = 3, 
                     method = "maximum")



fviz_cluster(k_2_euclid, data = scale(penguins_reduced), 
             main = sprintf("K = %d Clusters w/ Manhattan Distance", 3))







fviz_cluster(k_2_manattan, data = scale(penguins_reduced),
             main = sprintf("K = %d Clusters w/ Manhattan Distance", 3))







fviz_cluster(k_2_maxnorm, data = scale(penguins_reduced),
             main = sprintf("K = %d Clusters w/ Manhattan Distance", 3))








Try changing \(K\) to equal 3$ in the code chunk above. How do the clusterings using the 3 distance metrics compare? What do you generally observe?
Answer. YOUR ANSWER HERE
Modify the code in the chunk above so that we can easily change the value of K (rather than making sure to change K manually in every line). In general coding practices, is called extracting out a constant.

Cross Validation (CV)
Write a brief introduction to cross validation which includes relevant mathematical notation.
Answer: Cross validation is a statistical method used in machine learning to evaluate how well a model performs in an unseen or independent data set. It involves dividing the data set into multiple folds or subsets, using one of these folds as a validation set and training the model on the remaining folds. This process is then repeated multiple times each time using different fold as the validation set. The main purpose of cross validation is to prevent over fitting which occurs when a model is trained too well on the training data and performs poorly on new, unseen data
\(\mathrm{CV}(k) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^k \mathrm{MAE}_j\)
What is the goal of cross-validation? (Hint: Think about over-fitting, along with social/ethical considerations)
Answer: The goal of cross validation is to ensure that a model generalizes well beyond the data on which it was trained by repeatedly holding out different subsets fir testing, it guards against over fitting and produces an approximately unbiased estimate of out of sample error. This process not only helps in selecting and tuning models that truly capture underlying patterns rather than noise, but also promotes robustness and fairness: by validating across different folds.
What linear models are you considering based on your research question? Pick at least two models to compare.
Answer: I am considering two models. One model which is unadjusted model (model_1) which doesn’t contain confounders and another model which is adjusted model (model_2) that includes the confounders.
# Step 1: Model specification
lm_spec <- linear_reg() %>%
# Output Y is quantitative
set_mode("regression") %>%
# Want regression to be linear
set_engine("lm")
# Unadjusted model

  fit(gdpgrowth ~ oil, data = df_clean)
# Adjusted model
model_2 <- lm_spec %>% 
  fit(gdpgrowth ~ oil + school + invest, data = df_clean)
Explain how you divided your data into its test set and training set.
Answer: I split the data into two parts –a training set (80% of the observations) and a test set (the remaining 20%) so that we could both tune our models and then evaluate their performance on truly unseen data.
#split <- initial_split(df_clean, prop = 0.8, strata = "oil")

#test_data  <- testing(split)
State which error metric you are using (MAE or MSE) and give its formal mathematical definition. Why did you choose this error metric? What are the advantages/disadvantages of using it?
Answer: I will be using MAE. The formal mathematical definition is:
\(\mathrm{MAE} = \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n |y_i - \hat y_i|\)
I chose this error metric because it produces an error metric in the same units as the outcome which makes it immediately interpretable and it is also less sensitive to large outliers than the other error metric like MSE. The main advantage of MAE is the robustness to outliers. Since errors aren’t squared a few extreme misses don’t dominate the metric. Another advantage is that it’s easy to compute and understand which doesn’t require additional transformations.
However, it does have some drawbacks like MAE treats every error the same so one huge miss and several small misses can look equally bad even though we might just care about the big one.

text:
LASSO
Write a brief introduction to LASSO which includes relevant mathematical notation.
Answer: LASSO is a penalized regression method that shrinks coefficient estimates and performs variable selection.
\(\mathrm{RSS} + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j|\)
where lambda >= 0 is a tuning parameter controlling the strength of the L1 penalty. As lambda grows more coefficients are shrinking towards 0 or exactly to 0 which yields a model that is easier to interpret and often stable in the presence of multicollinearity. LASSO’s key advantages are it’s built in variable selection and improved predictive performance via regularization and it’s main drawback is potential bias in the non-zero coefficients due to shrinkage.
State which error metric you are using (i.e., CV MAE or CV MSE and state the chosen k-value).
Answer: I will me using CV MAE and k=10.
Identify at least p = 3 predictors X1, X2, …, Xp for modeling the expected response E(Y) of one of your variables Y.
Answer:
Compute 50 LASSO models for 50 different values of 𝜆 (the penalty tuning parameter), each with all p predictors. You can start out by trying 𝜆 in the range of -5 to 1 on the log10 scale. Plot the cross-validated (CV) error for each value of 𝜆.

  set_mode("regression") %>%
  set_engine("glmnet") %>%
  set_args(mixture = 1, penalty = tune())

  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())


# STEP 3: Workflow Specification (Model + Recipe)

  add_recipe(variable_recipe) %>%
  add_model(lasso_spec)


# STEP 4: Estimate 50 LASSO models using
# lambda values on a "grid" or range from 10^(-5) to 10^(-0.1).
# Calculate the 10-fold CV MAE for each of the 50 models.

  tune_grid(
    grid= grid_regular(penalty(range=c(-5,1)),levels= 50 ),
    resamples= vfold_cv(df_clean, v= 10 ),

    )
